paragraphs: “The medical experts have tried hard to convince us that the prisoner is out of his mind, that he is in fact a maniac. I say he is sane. If he were not, he would have acted more cleverly. That he is a maniac I will grant on one point only, his fixed idea about the three thousand. Even there, I think, a far simpler cause can be found than any tendency to madness. I agree entirely with the young doctor who held that the prisoner’s mind has always been sound, and that he has merely been irritable and exasperated. What kept the prisoner in such constant and violent anger was not the sum itself. Something particular lay underneath it. That something is jealousy!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch described at length the prisoner’s fatal passion for Grushenka. He began at the moment when the prisoner went to the “young person’s” lodgings “to beat her.” “Those are his own words,” the prosecutor explained. “But instead of beating her, he stayed on, at her feet. That is where the passion began. At the very same time, the prisoner’s father was captivated by the same young person. It was a strange and fatal coincidence. Both of them lost their hearts to her together, though each had known her before. In both she roused the most violent passion, a truly Karamazov passion. We have her own confession: ‘I was laughing at both of them.’ Yes, a sudden wish to make fun of them seized her, and she conquered them both at once. The old man, who worshiped money, immediately set aside three thousand roubles to pay for a single visit from her. Soon afterwards he would gladly have laid his fortune and his name at her feet, if only she would consent to be his lawful wife. We have good evidence of this. As for the prisoner, the tragedy of his fate is plain to see; it is before us. But that was the young person’s ‘game.’ The enchantress gave the unhappy young man no hope until the very last moment, when he knelt before her, holding out hands that were already stained with the blood of his father and his rival. He was arrested in that very posture. ‘Send me to Siberia with him! I brought him to this. I am the most to blame,’ the woman herself cried out, in real remorse, as he was arrested.

“Mr. Rakitin, the talented young man I mentioned earlier, summed up this heroine in a few striking words. ‘She was disillusioned early in life, deceived and ruined by a betrothed who seduced her and abandoned her. She was left in poverty and cursed by her respectable family. A rich old man took her under his protection, and she still regards him as her benefactor. There was perhaps much good in her young heart, but it was embittered too early. She grew prudent and saved her money. She grew sarcastic and resentful toward society.’ Given such a portrait, it is easy to see how she could laugh at the pair of them out of simple mischief, out of malice.

“For a month he loved without hope and sank morally lower. In that month he betrayed his betrothed and took money that had been entrusted to his honor. Constant jealousy drove the prisoner almost to frenzy, almost to madness. And jealous of whom? Of his own father! The worst of it was that the crazy old man was luring and tempting the woman the son loved with that very three thousand roubles. The son considered that money his own property, part of his inheritance from his mother, and he believed his father was cheating him out of it. Yes, I admit it was hard to bear! It could well drive a man mad. It was not the money that mattered, but the fact that it was being used, with such revolting cynicism, to ruin his happiness!”
Next the prosecutor described how the idea of murdering his father had first come into the prisoner’s head, and he supported his theory with facts.

“To begin with, he only talked of it in taverns, and he talked of it all through that month. Ah, he likes to have company around him all the time, and he likes to tell his companions everything, even his most diabolical and dangerous thoughts. He likes to share every idea with others. For some reason he expects those he confides in to meet him with perfect sympathy, to enter into all his troubles and worries, to take his side and never to oppose him in anything. If they do not, he flies into a rage and smashes up everything in the tavern. [Then followed the anecdote about Captain Snegiryov.] Those who heard the prisoner began to wonder at last whether he meant more than threats, and whether such a frenzy might turn threats into deeds.”

The prosecutor then recounted how the family had met at the monastery, what was said in the talks with Alyosha, and the horrible scene of violence when the prisoner burst into his father’s house straight after dinner.

“I cannot say for certain,” the prosecutor continued, “that the prisoner fully meant to murder his father before that incident. Yet the idea had come to him several times, and he had turned it over in his mind. For that we have facts, witnesses and his own words. I will admit to you, gentlemen of the jury,” he added, “that until today I was unsure whether to ascribe conscious premeditation to the prisoner. I was firmly convinced that he had pictured the fatal moment in advance, but that he had only pictured it, thinking of it as a possibility. When and how he might commit the crime, he had not yet decided.

“But I was unsure only until today, until that fatal document was laid before the court a moment ago. You heard for yourselves that young lady’s cry, ‘It is the plan, the program of the murder!’ That was her name for the unhappy prisoner’s wretched, drunken letter. And indeed that letter shows us that the whole murder was planned beforehand. It was written two days earlier. So we now know for a fact that, forty-eight hours before he carried out his terrible design, the prisoner swore that if he could not get money the next day, he would murder his father and take the envelope of notes from under his pillow, as soon as Ivan had gone. ‘As soon as Ivan had gone away.’ You hear that? He had thought everything through and weighed every circumstance, and he did it all exactly as he had written. The proof of premeditation is conclusive. The crime must have been committed for the money. That is stated plainly, written down and signed. The prisoner does not deny his signature.

“I shall be told that he was drunk when he wrote it. That takes nothing from the value of the letter, quite the contrary. Drunk, he wrote what he had planned sober. If he had not planned it sober, he would not have written it drunk. I shall be asked why, then, he talked about it in taverns. A man who premeditates such a crime keeps silent and says nothing to anyone. True, but he talked about it before he had a plan, when he had only the wish, only the impulse. Later he talked of it less. On the evening he wrote that letter at the ‘Metropolis’ tavern, he was silent, unlike his usual self, though he was drinking. He did not play billiards. He sat in a corner and spoke to no one. He did push a shopman out of his seat, but he did that almost without thinking, because he could never walk into a tavern without making a disturbance. It is true that once he had made his final decision, he must have feared that he had said too much about his plan in advance, and that it might lead to his arrest and prosecution afterwards. But there was nothing to be done. He could not take back his words. Yet his luck had served him before, and it would serve him again. He believed in his star, you know! And I must also admit that he did a great deal to avoid the fatal catastrophe. ‘Tomorrow I shall try to borrow the money from everyone,’ he writes, in his peculiar language, ‘and if they will not give it to me, there will be bloodshed.’”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch turned to a detailed account of all Mitya’s attempts to borrow the money. He described the visit to Samsonov and the journey to Lyagavy. “Harassed, jeered at, hungry, he had sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him, a likely story). He was tortured by jealousy at having left the object of his affections behind in the town, and he suspected she would go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away. At last he came back to the town, and to his joy found that she had not gone near his father. He took her himself to her protector. (Strange to say, he does not seem to have been jealous of Samsonov, which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his hiding place in the back gardens, and there he learns that Smerdyakov is in a fit and the other servant is ill. The coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals.’ What a temptation! Still he resists it. He goes to see a lady who has lived in our town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady had long followed his career with compassion. She gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, and the waste of his youth and strength in pot-house debauchery, and to set off for the gold mines of Siberia. ‘That would be an outlet for your turbulent energy, your romantic character, your thirst for adventure.’”

Ippolit Kirillovitch then described what came of this conversation. He described the moment when the prisoner learned that Grushenka had not stayed at Samsonov’s, and the sudden frenzy of the luckless man, worn out with jealousy and nervous exhaustion, at the thought that she had deceived him and was now with his father. He ended by dwelling on the fatal part played by chance. “If the maid had told him that her mistress was at Mokroe with her former lover, nothing would have happened. But she lost her head. All she could do was swear and protest that she knew nothing. The prisoner did not kill her on the spot only because he rushed off in pursuit of his faithless mistress.

“But note this. Frantic as he was, he took a brass pestle with him. Why that? Why not some other weapon? The answer is that he had been contemplating his plan and preparing for it for a whole month, so he would seize on anything that looked like a weapon. For a month past he had understood that any object of that kind would do as a weapon. So he recognized at once, without hesitation, that it would serve his purpose. It was by no means unconsciously, by no means involuntarily, that he snatched up that fatal pestle. And then we find him in his father’s garden. The coast is clear, there are no witnesses, there is darkness and jealousy. The suspicion that she was there, with him, with his rival, in his arms, and perhaps laughing at him at that very moment, took his breath away. And it was not mere suspicion. The deception was open and obvious. She must be there, in that lighted room, she must be behind the screen. Yet the unhappy man would have us believe that he crept up to the window, peeped politely in, and tactfully withdrew, for fear that something terrible and immoral might happen. He tries to persuade us of that, us, who understand his character, who know his state of mind at that moment, and who know that he knew the signals by which he could go straight into the house.” At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch broke off to discuss at length the suspected connection of Smerdyakov with the murder. He went into great detail, and everyone realized that, although he claimed to despise that suspicion, he thought the subject very important.
